title: Water conservation and environmental release for ponds
audience: Pond maintenance workers who top up, change or empty pond water, and who handle sludge, plants and fish during a service
learningOutcomes: Separate evaporation from a leak in a pond by carrying out a bucket test and recording the result
Limit unnecessary water changes and top-ups, and explain the cost and stress they create
Refuse to release pond water, sludge, plants or fish to stormwater, a waterway or bushland without an approved route and the permit the state requires
Record the volume moved, the route, the approval and the person who approved it

instruction.heading: Why pond water loss costs money
instruction.body: Every litre lost from a pond has to be replaced, and each top-up changes the water the fish and plants live in. Evaporation on a hot, windy day is normal. A steady loss on a cool, still night can point to a leak, an overflowing or misaligned outlet, or a waterfall that splashes water out of the pond. Unnecessary water changes cost money, add stress for fish, and can upset the bacteria that keep the filter working. Cost reduction starts with finding the cause of loss, rather than adding water every visit without knowing why.

instruction.heading: The bucket test and unnecessary changes
instruction.body: A simple bucket test separates evaporation from a leak. Place a bucket filled with pond water on a step within the pond, so that its water level is close to the pond's, and mark the level inside and outside the bucket at the start. Leave it for the same period, then compare the two marks. If the pond has dropped more than the water in the bucket, the loss is more likely a leak or an outlet problem, and it should be reported. The method is a practical technique and is not a certified test. Record the weather, the time and the result. Carry out a partial water change only when the test results, the client plan or a qualified specialist calls for one, and record the reason for it.

instruction.heading: Topping up with treated water
instruction.body: When a top-up is needed, add water that has had its chlorine and chloramine removed, because both harm fish and the bacteria in the filter. Add the top-up slowly and avoid pouring it onto fish or plants. Do not add water from an unknown source, such as a dam, bore or natural waterway, without checking the rules first.

instruction.heading: Releasing water, sludge, plants and fish
instruction.body: Pond water, sludge and removed plants must not be released into stormwater, a kerb drain, a gutter, bushland or a waterway unless the route has been confirmed in writing by the client, the council and the water authority. Councils regulate discharge routes for stormwater. One NSW council's factsheet treats discharging stormwater into the council sewer as an offence. That is a stormwater rule and does not decide the route for pond water. Fish are a separate matter. In Queensland, prohibited noxious fish cannot be brought in, and sightings of prohibited noxious fish and of sight-only restricted species have a 24-hour reporting limit to Biosecurity Queensland. For restricted fish such as carp and tilapia, the page says caught fish must be humanely killed straight away and disposed of away from water, and that they may not be kept, fed, given away, sold, used as bait or returned to water. In New South Wales, releasing fish into public waters such as rivers, creeks and impoundments needs a fish stocking permit under the Fisheries Management Act. The NSW page also places an abandoned pet fish in the same category as an abandoned cat or dog under section 11 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1979. Sludge and plant material may carry pest species and disease, so keep them on site until the approved disposal route is confirmed. Do not assume that any discharge route is allowed.

instruction.heading: Recording water movements
instruction.body: Record the volume drained, topped up or removed where you know it, the route, the approval or permit relied on, the time, the reason, and the person who approved the move. Where the route is unknown, stop and refer rather than moving the water. A record that shows the route was approved protects the business and the client, and a record that shows the water went somewhere unknown does neither.

procedure: Check the reason for water loss, and run a bucket test where the cause is not clear.
Record the weather, the test start and finish times, and the levels.
Report any suspected leak or outlet fault to the client and refer the repair.
Make a partial water change or top-up only where the test results or the client plan call for it, and record the reason.
Use water with chlorine and chloramine removed as the product label and the client plan direct.
Confirm the release route with the client, the council and the water authority before moving any water, sludge or plants.
Do not release fish. Refer any fish removal to the client and to the state rules for the species.
Record the volume, the route, the approval or permit and the person who approved it. Wear the PPE set by {{business:safety.required_ppe}} when handling sludge.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks you to drain the pond onto the front lawn and into the kerb drain because the water is green and they want it gone.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not drain to the lawn or the kerb drain. Explain the reason to the client, and say that the route must be confirmed with the council and the water authority first. Record the request, the refusal and the referral. If a partial change is needed for the green water, the plan decides the volume and the treated water used.

workedExamples.situation: A pond drops by a noticeable amount every night while the weather is still and cool, and the client asks for a top-up every visit.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not top up every visit without knowing why. Run a bucket test over a night, and compare the result with the weather. If the pond still drops more than the bucket, report a suspected leak or outlet fault and refer the repair. Record the test, the weather and the referral, so that the client can see why the top-ups were needed and the business can show the cost it saved.

equipmentAndPpe: Bucket for the bucket test and a marker for the water level
Dechlorinated water supply and product label for the treatment method
Sludge container with a lid for holding material on site
Gloves, eye protection and footwear with grip as set by {{business:safety.required_ppe}}

commonErrors.error: Topping up every visit without finding the cause of the loss.
commonErrors.prevention: Run a bucket test, record the weather and the result, and report a suspected leak.

commonErrors.error: Draining pond water to stormwater, a kerb drain or bushland without confirmed approval.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the route with the client, the council and the water authority in writing before moving any water.

commonErrors.error: Releasing a fish, or moving fish or plants between ponds, because the client asks.
commonErrors.prevention: Refuse the release and check the state rules. Record the request and the refusal.

commonErrors.error: Changing water on a fixed schedule rather than on the test results.
commonErrors.prevention: Carry out partial changes only where the results or the plan call for them, and record the reason.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: In Queensland, prohibited noxious fish cannot be brought in, and sightings must be reported within a 24-hour limit. Restricted fish, including carp and tilapia, may not be kept, fed, given away, sold or released. The state's detailed species list and any further rules are checked on the state page before action.

In New South Wales, releasing fish into public waters such as rivers, creeks and impoundments needs a fish stocking permit under the Fisheries Management Act, and possessing, buying, selling or moving the prohibited and notifiable species on the state schedules is illegal, with heavy penalties. The permit is separate from this lesson, and this lesson does not grant it.
The council's stormwater rule is one example of council control and does not decide the pond route. Confirm the route with the council and the water authority before any discharge.

qualityStandard: A bucket test or other cause check is recorded before a top-up is made on a repeat loss.
No water, sludge or plant material leaves the site without a confirmed route and an approval recorded.
No fish is released, moved or sold under this lesson.
documentationEvidence: Bucket test record with weather, times, levels and result
Top-up or partial change record with volume and the reason
Release route, approval or permit reference, and the approving person
Referral note for any suspected leak or outlet fault
summary: Find the cause of water loss with a bucket test before topping up.
Change water only where the results or the plan call for it, and record why.
Do not release pond water, sludge, plants or fish without a confirmed route and any permit the state requires.
Record the volume, the route, the approval and the approving person for every water movement.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client wants the pond emptied onto the lawn to save on water. What should you do?
options: Empty it, because it is only water and it will soak into the lawn quickly without causing any harm to the grass or the soil
Confirm the release route with the client, council and water authority first, and do not release fish or sludge
Empty it if the fish are removed to a bucket first, since the fish will be safe then and the water can go to the lawn
Empty it only when it is raining, since the rain will carry the water away from the lawn and the pond

knowledgeChecks.question: A pond drops by a noticeable amount every night in still, cool weather. What is the best first step?
options: Top it up every night without checking the cause, since the level must be kept full for the fish to survive
Empty half the pond and refill it, since the water will then be fresh and clean for the fish and plants
Run a bucket test to separate evaporation from a leak, then report a suspected leak if the loss continues
Add a water conditioner and wait a week, since the product should stop the loss of water from the pond

knowledgeChecks.question: A client in New South Wales asks you to release unwanted goldfish into a local creek. What is the correct response?
options: Release them, because goldfish are natural to waterways and will survive in the creek easily and happily
Release them only if they are small enough to be hidden in the reeds by the creek bank and not seen
Release them if the client signs a form that takes all responsibility for the release and the outcome
Refuse. Release into NSW public waters needs a fish stocking permit, and dumping an unwanted fish is an offence
